       REPLY OF NORTHERN VIRGINIA ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. TO
     RESPONSES TO INITIAL BRIEF OF PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C. AND TO
         INITIAL BRIEF AND JOINT RESPONSES OF THE INDICATED PJM
           TRANSMISSION OWNERS TO PAPER HEARING QUESTIONS

         Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) December 18,

2025 order (“Co-Location Order”),1 Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“NOVEC”)

respectfully submits this reply to the responses to the initial briefs and joint responses to the

paper hearing questions submitted by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”)2 and the Indicated

PJM Transmission Owners (“PJM Transmission Owners”).3




1
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, PP 219-20 (2025) (“Co-Location Order”); see also PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C., Notice of Extension of Time, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (Jan. 23, 2026) (Accession
No. 20260123-3062) (Extending the due date for responses to initial briefs by seven days, from April 17, 2026, to
April 24, 2026).
2

20260223-5189) (“PJM Initial Brief”).
3
  Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, Initial Brief and Joint Responses of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners,
Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (filed Feb. 23, 2026) (Accession No. 20260223-5190) (“PJM TO Initial Brief”).

                                                        2
                                        I.       INTRODUCTION

        When the Commission issued the Co-Location Order4 ordering PJM to provide new

transmission services to accommodate serving Co-Located Loads, the Commission left

implementation details to be developed through this paper hearing. PJM and the PJM

Transmission Owners have addressed many, but not all, of the necessary implementation details.

NOVEC disagreed5 and continues to disagree that any new transmission service should be

formulated for Co-Located Loads rather than requiring them to use Network Integration

Transmission Service (“NITS”), largely because it is not just or reasonable for other transmission

customers to subsidize Co-Located Load. But, respecting that the Commission has decided to

require the development of these new variations of transmission service, NOVEC generally

supported the proposals of PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners because they are designed to

prevent existing transmission customers from subsidizing Co-Located Load.6

        The responses to the initial briefs demonstrate that additional clarity is needed on certain

threshold issues regarding which kinds of entities are or are not Eligible Customers (including

whether a Load Serving Entity (“LSE”) like NOVEC can be required to serve as an Eligible

Customer if a Co-Located Load or generator serving Co-Located Load were to interconnect to

NOVEC’s distribution system in order to access the PJM transmission system), as well as

Commission guidance on other aspects of the rates, terms, and conditions of the new

transmission services. NOVEC’s comments focus on threshold issues relating to who is or must




4
  See Co-Location Order.
5
  NOVEC, Protest, Docket No. EL25-20-000 (filed Dec. 18, 2024) (Accession No. 20241218-5285); see also
NOVEC, Response to Initial Briefs, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (filed Mar. 25, 2026) (Accession No.
20260325-5220”) (“NOVEC Brief”).
6

                                                      3
 be an Eligible Customer and on a number of issues relating to the rates, terms, and conditions of

the new transmission services that require additional development.

        As explained below, NOVEC respectfully requests that the Commission provide

additional guidance on who may act as an Eligible Customer. NOVEC also requests that the

Commission: (1) approve the use of the NITS rate for Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission

Service (“Non-Firm CDS”); (2) approve PJM’s proposal to restrict a Co-Located Load receiving

Interim NITS from taking energy and capacity from the co-located generating facility when the

Co-Located Load is curtailed; (3) confirm that there should be a Grid Reliance Charge; (4)

consider the financial penalty proposal of the PJM Transmission Owners, subject to additional

details; and (5) approve an effective date that allows all parties involved to prepare for providing

services to Co-Located Load.

                                              II.      ANSWER

        A. The Commission should make clear who may or must act as an Eligible
           Customer and address related questions about the terms of service.

        There are unanswered questions regarding the definition and role of Eligible Customer

for purposes of the new transmission services for Co-Located Load. The Co-Location Order

provides that it is the Eligible Customer that will take transmission service on behalf of the Co-

Located Load.7 The PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”), consistent with the pro

forma tariff under Order No. 888, defines Eligible Customer as follows:

                 (i) Any electric utility … or any person generating electric energy for sale
                 for resale … (ii) Any retail customer taking unbundled transmission service
                 pursuant to a state requirement that the Transmission Provider or a
                 Transmission Owner offer the transmission service, or pursuant to a
                 voluntary offer of such service by a Transmission Owner, is an Eligible
                 Customer under the Tariff . . . .8

7
  Co-Location Order at PP 175-176; id. at n.379 (“…the replacement rate we establish in Part IV.B.4 applies to
Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Load….”).
8
  PJM Tariff, Part I, § 1, Definitions E-F.

                                                         4
 The Commission expanded on that definition in the Co-Location Order, stating that an Eligible

Customer could be “for example, any person generating electric energy for resale or any retail

customer taking unbundled transmission service under certain conditions…,”9 or that “subject to

applicable state law, the Eligible Customer could create a corporate intermediary to serve the Co-

Located Load, or the Co-Located Load, acting as an Eligible Customer, could request service

from the relevant transmission owner directly”10 while referring back to the PJM Tariff

definition for “the full definition of Eligible Customer….”11

        Several parties raised a question about who can act as an Eligible Customer. Invenergy

Renewables LLC and Invenergy Thermal LLC (collectively, “Invenergy”) asked the

Commission to confirm that “where a state retail choice program results in unbundled retail

access, customers may take transmission service as an Eligible Customer[,]” effectively asking

when a Co-Located Load could qualify as an Eligible Customer.12 Old Dominion Electric

Cooperative (“ODEC”) sought clarification as to whether it would have to provide authorization

under circumstances where it is the Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”).13

        The Commission should consider a more definitive delineation of who may be an

Eligible Customer as well as the scope of the Eligible Customer’s obligations. NOVEC also

seeks confirmation that it cannot be required to serve as an Eligible Customer serving Co-

Located Load unless it agrees to do so. In the Co-Location Order, the Commission gives agency

to the Eligible Customers who may “at their option, take a new interim, non-firm transmission

 service until all Network Upgrades necessary to provide NITS are complete” if the Eligible

Customer is seeking to provide NITS or the Eligible Customer “can choose to take [Firm or Non-

Firm CDS] on behalf of a Co-Located Load instead of taking NITS.”14

            NOVEC is an electric distribution cooperative and LSE that serves many of the data

centers in “Data Center Alley” in Northern Virginia, sometimes referred to as the “Data Center

Capital of the World.” NOVEC needs to understand what obligations, if any, the Commission is

intending to impose on LSEs with respect to Co-Located Load that seeks to use the new

transmission services required by the Co-Location Order. NOVEC is not a PJM Transmission

Owner but does own and operate a significant distribution system which has numerous points of

interconnection with the transmission system in PJM’s Dominion transmission pricing zone.

NOVEC relies on PJM NITS to serve all of its load, including its very significant and constantly

growing data center load.

           NOVEC is an Eligible Customer under the PJM Tariff’s existing definition of that term,

but seeks clarification of its obligations under the Co-Location Order to act as an Eligible

Customer on behalf of a Co-Located Load in the event one were to interconnect to NOVEC’s

distribution system and wish to use these new transmission services:

           (1) Is a Co-Located Load eligible for these new transmission services if it interconnects

               to an LSE’s distribution infrastructure rather than directly to the transmission system?

           (2) Even assuming that a Co-Located Load that is interconnected to distribution

               infrastructure that is not dedicated to or part of the PJM transmission system is

               eligible to use these new services under the PJM Tariff, NOVEC seeks confirmation




14
     Co-Location Order at P 160.

                                                    6
                   that the Commission is not requiring an LSE like NOVEC to serve as an Eligible

                  Customer on behalf of the Co-Located Load unless it voluntarily elects to do so.

           Requiring an LSE like NOVEC to serve as an Eligible Customer on behalf of a Co-

Located Load carries many complications. From a legal standpoint, because the states determine

who may provide retail service, sales to the Co-Located Load as the end-user must be authorized

under state law and the Co-Located Load cannot be an Eligible Customer unless state law allows

it to take unbundled transmission service.15 The Commission of course must respect state

jurisdiction over retail rates, which means, inter alia, that the Commission cannot require LSEs

to modify their retail rates to accommodate these new service and undertake the administrative

burden of being an Eligible Customer for a Co-Located Load unless the LSE chooses to do so.

           From a compliance and liability standpoint, LSEs like NOVEC should not be subject to

potential liability for the transmission costs, much less penalties for non-compliance with the

Tariff’s requirements, if a Co-Located Load for which NOVEC is serving as Eligible Customer

fails to meet or comply with all applicable provisions of these services, including curtailing load

when required to do so. Operationally, NOVEC is uncertain as to how the Co-Located Load

might be curtailed without potentially creating operational constraints that are highly sensitive to

the timing and frequency of curtailment notifications. In particular, frequent notices or ones that

are insufficiently in advance of required implementation could hinder effective operational

planning and resource allocation. Consideration of these dynamics is important to mitigate

potential disruptions and maintain reliable system operations.

           From a practical and PJM Tariff standpoint, if an LSE relies on NITS to serve its load, it

is NOVEC’s understanding that the Co-Located Load would have to be electrically isolated from



15
     Id. P 168.

                                                      7
 the remainder of the LSE’s network load if the Co-Located Load seeks to use Firm CDS, Non-

Firm CDS, or Interim NITS, because typically an LSE cannot use NITS for only a portion of its

load unless that portion is electrically isolated from the balance of the LSE’s load.16 Electrically

isolating such Load would require physical and electrical configurations that would be unique to

that of Co-Located Load and could require significant upgrades or additions.

        NOVEC believes that utilities should be prepared to serve all customers within their

authorized service areas, but NOVEC is concerned about the implications of being required to

procure transmission service other than NITS to meet the load it serves. Absent a compelling

benefit to its customers or arrangements that fully protect other customers from any adverse costs

or operational impact arising out of service to Co-Located Load, NOVEC would rather not act as

an Eligible Customer serving Co-Located Load for any service other than NITS. NOVEC

respectfully requests that the Commission confirm that that NOVEC is not obligated to apply for

Firm CDS, Non-Firm CDS, or Interim NITS on behalf of Co-Located Load that is interconnected

to NOVEC’s distribution facilities or connected to Dominion but within NOVEC’s service area.

        B. The Commission should address questions raised during the proceeding
           regarding the rates, terms, and conditions of Firm CDS, Non-Firm CDS, and
           Interim NITS.

                 1. The Commission should approve the use of the NITS rate for Non-Firm
                    CDS.

        The PJM Transmission Owners proposed charging the NITS rate for Non-Firm CDS.17 In

responsive briefs, several participants indicated opposition to the use of the NITS rate for Non-

Firm CDS.18 NOVEC supported the proposal and continues to support this proposal. Non-Firm

customer may not designate only part of the load at a discrete Point of Delivery as Network Load).

 CDS “is a transmission service that allows an Eligible Customer taking service on behalf of Co-

Located Loads to obtain non-firm, interruptible transmission service on behalf of a Co-Located

Load in the event the Co-Located Generating Facility is on outage and unable to provide any of

the dedicated level of energy….”19 Under PJM’s proposal, it is only available when the generator

is on outage. Reservations are available “for terms ranging from one hour to one month,

consistent with the terms available for non-firm [Point-to-Point Service (“PTPS”)] currently in

the PJM Tariff.”20 As proposed by the PJM Transmission Owners, “the maximum rate for Non-

Firm Contract Demand Service on behalf of Co-Located Load will be calculated by multiplying

(i) their reserved, non-firm contract demand amount (in MWs) by (ii) the applicable zonal NITS

rate.”21 The Non-Firm CDS customer will also receive an adjustment to reflect the impact of the

Grid Reliance Charge in order to prevent double-recovery.22

        Based on the design proposed by the PJM Transmission Owners, the intention behind the

proposal is to charge Non-Firm CDS customers only when they make a reservation to use

transmission capacity on an as-available basis. This is reflected in the PJM Transmission

Owners’ request for clarification that “an Eligible Customer’s initial application for a certain

amount of Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service would essentially serve as a

‘holding’ request, and the actual reservation and use of Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service would require the Eligible Customer to submit individual requests for

service in advance of the interval during which it wishes to obtain such service.”23 The PJM

(Accession No. 20260325-5236) (“Joint Co-Location Developers Brief”).

 Transmission Owners added that “the amount that PJM determines is available for a particular

requested interval or intervals would presumably serve as the basis for determining the relevant

charge to the Eligible Customer for Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service.”24 The

PJM Transmission Owners concluded by asking PJM to “confirm [that] these understandings are

correct and add appropriate language to its proposed Tariff provisions.”25

        Some of the opposition appears to come from a misapprehension of the proposal, which

illustrates why the request for clarification by the PJM Transmission Owners should be granted.

Geronimo Power, LLC (“Geronimo Power”) suggests by way of example that a “100 MW load

co-located with a 100 MW generator located within a zone with a NITS and Firm Contract

Demand transmission service rate of $10,000/MW/year and a Grid Reliance Charge of

$2,580/MW/Year” would “pay the same amount if it reserved 100 MW of Firm Contract

Demand transmission service or 100 MW of Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission

service.”26 But, under PJM’s proposal, Geronimo Power’s hypothetical customer would only

take and pay for Non-Firm CDS when the generator was experiencing an outage. Even under an

alternative scenario where Eligible Customers had greater flexibility to mix and match Firm and

Non-Firm CDS, the Eligible Customer would only pay for the actual Non-Firm CDS it receives

to cover whatever it chooses not to generate or procure through Firm CDS. In contrast, the

customer would pay for Firm Contract Demand Service throughout the term of its reservation

regardless of its usage. The same rate thus does not equate to the same cost to the customer, as

Geronimo Power seems to argue.

         Other opposition to the proposal is rooted in a flawed analysis of Commission precedent

and the cost-causation principle or an appeal to policy reasons. The cost-causation principle

requires that all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer

who must pay them, and the courts “evaluate compliance with this unremarkable principle by

comparing the costs assessed against a party to the burdens imposed or benefits drawn by that

party.”27 While adhesion to the cost causation principle does not require “exacting precision,” the

Commission must have an “articulable and plausible reason” to believe that the benefits are

roughly commensurate with costs.28

        Various parties argue that Non-Firm CDS service imposes lesser costs on the grid that

should warrant a discount.29 This premise remains unproven. When the Co-Located Load is

using Non-Firm CDS and is not curtailed, its use of the transmission system is comparable to the

way NITS customers use it. Unlike a point-to-point transmission service product, Non-Firm CDS

is not restricted to designated sources and sinks. And although under PJM’s construct Non-Firm

CDS is only available when the generator is experiencing an outage, that may occur more

frequently than expected. In its reply brief, the Independent Market Monitor for PJM (“IMM”)

pointed out that “[g]enerators providing co-located service will not be available for 8,760 hours

per year.”30 Rather, the availability factor for other PJM generators “was 83.2 percent…in 2025”

and “the system would become unmanageable if all or a significant part of the data center users

wanted to use non-firm CDS….”31 Unlike NITS, which “ensures the system overall is

‘proactively’ planned to a forecasted level of service and the needed resource capacity to

Electric Cooperative v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1255 (D.C. Cir. 2018).

   Illinois Commerce Commission v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 477 (7th Cir. 2009).

 maintain the reliability of service is secured ahead of time[,]” Non-Firm CDS is not accounted

for in models and will appear on the system frequently, but irregularly.32 PJM faces significant

challenges in planning to ensure that this can be done reliably.33

         Rather than contend that Non-Firm CDS imposes lesser costs on the transmission system

than NITS, it would be fairer to say that it imposes costs differently. It is true that PJM will not

be building upgrades to accommodate requests for Non-Firm CDS, but PJM will now be faced

with the prospect of receiving and managing these requests (for as much as 20 percent of the

time) for short-term transmission service. And the anticipated frequency of these requests based

on generators’ likely downtime points to a greater use and reliance on the transmission system

than the other parties represent.34 The Commission needs to be cautious to avoid providing “co-

located generators a subsidized low cost option to use the system whenever they need backup.”35

Part of what NITS customers pay for is the ability to use the transmission system when needed.

         The Commission should disfavor the argument that because Non-Firm CDS is a lower

priority than NITS it should necessarily have a lower cost. The practical reality is that Co-

Located Load can game the system if the Commission accepts that premise. As part of the

application for Non-Firm CDS, PJM studies how much it can reliably provide. If the Co-Located

Load is unhappy with that result, it always has the option to request Interim NITS, NITS, or Firm

CDS. Co-Located Load in areas where PJM can accommodate a large amount of Non-Firm CDS

could end up with the best of both worlds, where they are very rarely curtailed but pay a

subsidized rate for transmission service. If PJM later determines it can no longer accommodate

NITS at that point. Choosing to accept the risk of curtailment could simply reflect the de minimis

nature of that risk. Accordingly, the Commission should not sanction a discount from NITS

simply because the risk of curtailment exists.

        Vistra argues that Non-Firm CDS should receive the same rate as non-firm PTPS

customers because both services are non-firm.36 The Commission should reject this argument. In

addition to a differing level of firmness,37 Non-Firm CDS differs from non-firm PTPS because it

is not a point-to-point service, which Vistra does not acknowledge. It would not be appropriate to

allow Non-Firm CDS the same discount as non-firm PTPS because the two products

fundamentally differ.

        The Commission has said that non-firm transmission services may be charged at the same

rate as NITS.38 The PJM Transmission Owners have adequately supported their proposal. The

PJM Transmission Owners explained that Non-Firm CDS will “represent a superior level of

service compared to non-firm PTPS.”39 In addition to that superior level of service, Non-Firm

CDS have greater flexibility and do not have to pay for generation capacity.40 Those benefits,

coupled with the potential reliability concerns and gaming issues, demonstrate that the NITS rate

satisfies the cost-causation principle for use as the Non-Firm CDS rate.

        The PJM Transmission Owners further explained that “[b]efore determining whether a

discount is appropriate for Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, and if so what level it should be

Contract Demand Service customers are utilizing the service, taking into account the intended

purpose of the service, and the effect of that utilization on the system.”41 NOVEC agrees that

before a discount is set, it is appropriate to consider how Non-Firm CDS customers are using the

service and the effect of their utilization on the system. Without that practical experience, no one

can reasonably determine whether a discount is appropriate. If the Commission were to pre-

emptively order a discounted rate, the Commission would effectively be forcing existing

transmission customers—which includes ordinary people struggling with affordability

concerns—to bear the risk that they will subsidize large loads. In addition to the impact of

transmission upgrades to accommodate large loads that are socialized to all transmission

customers, large loads may also have an impact on aspects of PJM markets. NOVEC respectfully

submits that as between the two types of customers that could bear that risk, the customer that

should bear the risk of any mistake should be the ones receiving a special privilege to facilitate

their service. The Federal Power Act is a consumer-protection statute; therefore, the Commission

should protect the consumer, institute the NITS rate for Non-Firm CDS, and reserve the question

for a future filing by the PJM Transmission Owners.

           Finally, the Joint Co-Location Developers argue that the proposed rate would “discourage

productive industrial development, if adopted.”42 It is the Commission’s obligation to ensure that

rates are just and reasonable, not to provide subsidies to select, power-intensive industries at the

expense of ordinary consumers. If some industries are not viable without subsidization by other

customers, it is not the Commission’s role to provide them subsidies at the expense of

transmission customers at-large.

                  2. When a Co-Located Load using Interim NITS is curtailed, it should not
                    be able to take energy from the co-located generating facility.

        After filing its initial brief, PJM explained in a March 16, 2026, stakeholder presentation

that Co-Located Load taking Interim NITS will not have the rights to the capacity and energy

from any specific co-located generation in its proposed Interim NITS construct when curtailed.43

Many commenters objected to this aspect of PJM’s proposal.44 The arguments boil down to an

assertion that the lack of those rights defeats the purpose of co-location or makes Interim NITS

unworkable or unfair in some way. These arguments are without merit and should be

disregarded.

        Interim NITS is a temporary service provided while the transmission system is prepared

to provide full NITS to the Co-Located Load. What is important to remember is that the end goal

is NITS—the Co-Located Load is in that sense no different than any other large load. Proximity

of a generator to the load is irrelevant when the Co-Located Load is being served under network
